content: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection has been associated with various malignant and non-malignant conditions, including peptic ulcers, non-ulcer dyspepsia, recurrent peptic ulcer bleeding, unexplained iron deficiency anemia, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and colorectal adenomas. The definitive diagnosis of H. pylori infection is typically achieved through endoscopic biopsy, followed by histopathological examination. This examination often employs hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining or specialized stains such as Giemsa or Warthin-Starry stains, with the latter being more accurate than H&E staining. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding the diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive tests for detecting H. pylori. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive tests, including the urea breath test, serology, and stool antigen test, either individually or in combination, for diagnosing H. pylori infection in both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals. This is critical for initiating appropriate eradication therapy for H. pylori. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, the Science Citation Index, and the National Institute for Health Research Health Technology Assessment Database. The search was last updated on December 4, 2016. No restrictions were placed on language, publication status, or whether the data were collected prospectively or retrospectively. Diagnostic accuracy studies were included if they evaluated at least one of the index tests (urea breath test using isotopes such as 13C or 14C, serology, or stool antigen test) against the reference standard of histopathological examination using H&E stain, special stains, or immunohistochemical stains. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the methodological quality using the QUADAS-2 tool. Meta-analyses were performed using the hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model to estimate and compare SROC curves. Where appropriate, bivariate or univariate logistic regression models were used to estimate summary sensitivities and specificities. The analysis included 101 studies with a total of 11,003 participants, of whom 5,839 (53.1%) were diagnosed with H. pylori infection. The prevalence of H. pylori infection across the studies ranged from 15.2% to 94.7%, with a median prevalence of 53.7%. Most studies (57%) included participants with dyspepsia, and 53 studies excluded individuals who had recently used proton pump inhibitors or antibiotics. Each study had at least some risk of bias or concerns about applicability. Among the 101 studies, 15 compared the accuracy of two index tests, and two studies compared the accuracy of three index tests. Specifically, 34 studies (4,242 participants) evaluated serology, 29 studies (2,988 participants) evaluated the stool antigen test, 34 studies (3,139 participants) evaluated the urea breath test using 13C, 21 studies (1,810 participants) evaluated the urea breath test using 14C, and two studies (127 participants) evaluated the urea breath test without specifying the isotope used. The thresholds for test positivity and the staining techniques for histopathological examination varied between studies, making it difficult to identify the optimal threshold for each test. Using data from 99 studies, an indirect comparison revealed statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy among the urea breath test (13C and 14C), serology, and stool antigen test (P = 0.024). The diagnostic odds ratios (DORs) were as follows: 153 (95% CI 73.7 to 316) for the urea breath test-13C, 105 (95% CI 74.0 to 150) for the urea breath test-14C, 47.4 (95% CI 25.5 to 88.1) for serology, and 45.1 (95% CI 24.2 to 84.1) for the stool antigen test. At a fixed specificity of 0.90, the sensitivity was estimated to be 0.94 (95% CI 0.89 to 0.97) for the urea breath test-13C, 0.92 (95% CI 0.89 to 0.94) for the urea breath test-14C, 0.84 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.91) for serology, and 0.83 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.90) for the stool antigen test. In a hypothetical cohort of 1,000 individuals with a prevalence of H. pylori infection of 53.7% and a specificity of 0.90, there would be 46 false positives (individuals without H. pylori infection who are incorrectly diagnosed as infected). The number of false negatives (individuals with H. pylori infection who are missed) would be 30 (95% CI 15 to 58) for the urea breath test-13C, 42 (95% CI 30 to 58) for the urea breath test-14C, 86 (95% CI 50 to 140) for serology, and 89 (95% CI 52 to 146) for the stool antigen test. Direct comparisons of diagnostic accuracy were limited, with only a few head-to-head studies available. The ratios of DORs were 0.68 (95% CI 0.12 to 3.70; P = 0.56) for the urea breath test-13C versus serology (seven studies) and 0.88 (95% CI 0.14 to 5.56; P = 0.84) for the urea breath test-13C versus the stool antigen test (seven studies). The confidence intervals for these estimates overlapped with those from the indirect comparisons, and data for other direct comparisons were sparse or unavailable. In conclusion, urea breath tests (13C and 14C) demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for detecting H. pylori infection in individuals without a history of gastrectomy or recent use of antibiotics or proton pump inhibitors. Serology and stool antigen tests were less accurate. However, the thresholds for test positivity varied widely, and no specific thresholds could be recommended for clinical practice. Further high-quality comparative studies are needed to provide more reliable evidence on the relative accuracy of these tests. Such studies should be conducted prospectively in representative populations, with clearly reported thresholds and minimal risk of bias.
